Italdizain · Everything for Home
Architect's brief — Baku, August 2026 — revised v3 — private & confidential

Build us a home.

Door 01 of Italdizain's new Everything for Home chain. Its address is Fountain Square Passage, at the centre of Baku White City. This document is the working brief for our collaboration with you: what the place is, how the floor divides, and — most importantly — how we want furniture and décor to be presented in a way no one else in Baku presents them. A commercially driven everything-for-home concept — with an identity entirely its own. The brand itself — name, mark, voice — is being created in parallel; this brief defines the space it will live in.

An interactive document. Click the category bar to open each zone, switch the module tabs, and reveal the plan layers one by one. Reading time ≈ 15 minutes.

01

The place.

Baku White City

White City is the most ambitious urban redevelopment in the region — a high-end residential and business district built just east of the city centre, planned around walkability, premium architecture and a structured street grid, with new residential blocks, Class A offices and hotels still coming out of the ground. It is where Baku's affluent families are moving, and where they furnish new apartments. That last point is the reason we are going there.

Fountain Square Passage

A boutique shopping centre at the heart of the district: three trading levels, direct pedestrian entrances on all sides, a two-level car park below, and the landing point of the cable-stayed pedestrian bridge that connects White City to the Boulevard National Park on the Caspian shoreline. The mall is deliberately positioned as a "destination", founded on a portfolio of leading home décor and furniture brands — this boutique is meant to be one of the anchors of that thesis, not a tenant hiding in it.

Who walks in

Weekdays: White City residents plus staff from the surrounding Class A offices — errand traffic, gifting, top-up purchases. Weekends: a high-spending clientele from across Baku, drawn by an offer they cannot find elsewhere, plus international visitors crossing the bridge from the Boulevard. The mall's own positioning targets the affluent, design-aware customer who wants a "lifestyle" venue to see and be seen in. The interior must reward both modes: fast, legible shopping on weekdays; browsing, discovery and staging on weekends.

The architecture we sit inside

Contemporary stone-clad volumes, generous glazing, a skylit steel-framed galleria, curved terraced façades, panoramic terraces, and the sculptural bridge as the signature gesture. Daylight and long sightlines are part of the building's character. Our interior should converse with this — calm, precise, material-led — rather than fight it with noise. We are the quiet, confident room inside an expressive building.

02

The space.

The boutique is planned at roughly 1,000 m² of trading area. The split below is our current category allocation — it is a commercial instruction, not a floor plan. How these shares become adjacencies, aisles and sightlines is exactly what we are asking you to design. Click any segment.

click a segment to open its zone

The extension option

To the right of the main entrance there is a realistic possibility to extend the boutique beyond its current line. We want to reserve that zone, in the concept, for outdoor & garden furniture and for the Christmas shop in season. Note the arithmetic: Seasonal (10%) plus Outdoor & Garden (7%) is ≈ 170 m² — if the extension is confirmed, most of that programme migrates out of the core floor and returns ≈ 17% of the main sales area to furniture, moods and tabletop.

Please treat the extension as a design contingency: the core plan must work without it, and gain — not reshuffle — when it arrives. The two seasonal programmes should be able to swap dress (garden in summer, Christmas from October) on the same fixture skeleton.

And note: Outdoor & Garden is a commercial category, not a styling exercise. Beyond outdoor furniture it may include garden furniture, garden tools, lawn-care equipment, lawnmowers and related outdoor-living products. The display language must handle technical products while remaining unmistakably ours — and still convert seasonally into the Christmas shop.

03

One shop.
Two languages.

The floor divides into two display logics that must read as one boutique. This is the central idea of the brief — everything else is detail.

Language A — the system

Benchmarks, not templates

Kitchen & Dining, Home Textile, Household and small Appliances — roughly 480 m², nearly half the floor — run on one coherent fixture system. No single retailer should define it. Golden Apple is a behavioural benchmark only — for energy, discovery, circulation and impulse behaviour — never a visual or architectural reference. Draw instead on a broader set: CoinCasa for merchandising efficiency and replenishment; Zara Home for styling and visual editing; IKEA for planning and service logic; Maisons du Monde for mixing furniture, décor and accessible room inspiration. Extract principles, never copy a store. The boutique must have its own architectural language, material palette, detailing, finishes and customer experience.

Kitchen & Dining · 250 m² Home Textile · 130 m² Household · 80 m² Appliances · 20 m²
Language B — the moods

Custom mood modules

Furniture & Décor — 350 m², the single largest category — is to be presented in a way that exists nowhere else in Baku: a sequence of 15–20 m² "mini moods". Each mood is a small, complete domestic world: a hero furniture setting at its centre or corner, wrapped by two walls of shelving and showcases carrying the alternative pieces and the décor that belong to that world. Not room sets behind a rope — shoppable rooms where every object on every shelf is for sale. Section 04 specifies this module in full; it is the heart of the brief.

Furniture & Décor · 350 m² + bed textiles woven in
The guest — branded corner

Villeroy & Boch — 70 m²

Inside the boutique there will be a 70 m² Villeroy & Boch corner — a branded shop-in-shop, built to V&B's corner identity and fixture guidelines. Italdizain is Villeroy & Boch's retail partner in Azerbaijan, so the brand package (fixtures, graphics, merchandising rules) comes through us; your task is to place it and to resolve its boundary.

Position it within or directly beside Kitchen & Dining — V&B tabletop must borrow footfall from, and lend authority to, the rest of the tableware floor. The corner keeps its own identity, but its threshold with the wider boutique environment must feel seamless: continuous circulation, coherent flooring and lighting, and no dead edge.

The seam between the two languages matters as much as the languages themselves. A customer should drift from a kitchenware bay into a dining mood without noticing a border — same floor, same light temperature, same signage voice. Propose the transition; do not let the shop become two shops.

04

The mood module.

What we mean, in one image

The reference beside this text shows the intent. In the middle: a styled living setting — sofa, armchair, coffee table, rug, styled and lit like a home. Around it: full-height merchandised walls where décor, cushions, lamps, baskets and even accent chairs sit on the shelves themselves, each with its price, dense but curated. The setting seduces; the walls sell. The customer falls for the room, then finds every variation of it within arm's reach.

If anything in this section is ambiguous, ask us before designing around the ambiguity — this display concept is the one thing we will not compromise by accident.

The shelf wall, in elevation

The rules of the module

01

Footprint 15–20 m². As many as fit.

Within the ≈ 350 m² Furniture & Décor zone, plan as many modules as the geometry honestly allows after circulation — our expectation is in the order of 12–16. Density of worlds beats size of worlds; do not inflate modules to fill space.

02

One hero setting per mood, centre or corner.

The main furniture of the mood — fully styled, layered, lit like a home, standing on its rug. It defines the style; it is the photograph the customer takes. It is also entirely shoppable.

03

Two walls of shelves and showcases — repetition and comparison.

The perimeter sells by repetition and comparison, not by scarcity. A full row of chairs, one after another, on a single shelf; a row of sofas lined up beneath them; then dedicated showcases — one for the décor of the mood (vases, candles, frames, books, trays, cushions, throws), one for coffee tables, side and nesting tables, stools, ottomans, benches, small consoles, mirrors and lamps — the small furniture of the living room, shelved. Long runs, price rails, effortless like-for-like comparison. Luxury lives in the product and in the finish of the fixture; the display works by repetition and easy comparison.

04

Beds: one hero, a headboard / material gallery.

Bedroom moods follow the same skeleton, with one exception — we will not line up full beds from stock. One hero bed, dressed to seduce; beside it a headboard / material gallery where customers choose the head, fabric and finish (mounted vertically, swatch logic, clearly ordered). And note carefully: bed textiles are merchandised inside the bedroom moods — linen, covers, cushions and throws styled on the bed and stocked on the mood's shelves. Part of the Home Textile programme therefore physically lives in Language B; coordinate the split with us so nothing is counted twice.

05

Dining tables: an open question, addressed to you.

Tables are the hardest furniture to show — big, flat, repetitive. We have not solved this and we want your proposal. Directions we would test: a single dressed hero table per dining mood with alternative tabletops displayed vertically on a rail (edge-on, like large-format tiles), with corner and leg samples at hand; a compact "table gallery" where two or three tables of different character stand in a row, each half-dressed to show both the surface and the mise en place; or a materials-and-bases library wall paired with one hero. Bring us the version you believe in — or a better one.

06

Built to be re-dressed.

Moods rotate — seasonally at minimum, faster when a collection lands. The skeleton must survive every rotation without tools or trades: adjustable shelves, movable plinths, track lighting, a mood identity band that swaps in minutes. Design the module as an instrument, not a stage set.

07

Open fronts, honest prices, no theatre ropes.

Customers walk into the mood, sit on the sofa, open the drawers. Price communication is calm and present on every object — the reference image's discipline, in our own voice.

Part of the sales floor

Home Consultation / Planning Area

Provide a dedicated, customer-facing planning area within or immediately adjacent to Furniture & Décor. It must support 60–90 minute consultations: a proper working table, comfortable chairs, a screen or monitor, catalogue storage and an organised library of fabric, finish and material samples. It is part of the sales floor, not a back office — customers should see planning happening, and leave wanting an appointment of their own.

05

Showcases & selling moments.

Six display types cover the whole assortment. Each product family should always know which type it lives on — that mapping is the merchandising grammar of the boutique.

Wall bay — the system

House-developed wall shelving — adjustable, dense, replenishable, equipped for clear price communication.

For: cookware, glassware, porcelain, household, small appliances.

Tavola table

Presentation table set as a complete mise en place, changed with the season.

For: tableware stories, seasonal table, gifting.

Gondola & island

Mid-floor double-sided units; folded stock by colour; browse-height only.

For: home textile stock, bath, everyday household.

Vitrine

Glazed, locked, lit showcase — the Royal Collection instinct applied to the home.

For: crystal, silver, premium porcelain, high-value gifts.

Mood shelf wall

Language B perimeter — décor plus shelf-scale furniture in lit niches (Section 04).

For: décor, lamps, accent chairs, side tables, cushions, throws.

Plinth cluster

Stepped plinths at decision points — the "window" logic carried inside the shop.

For: hero objects, new arrivals, campaign pieces.
Selling moment — the till

Checkout = Gifting / Party / Impulse zone

The cash desk must be an active selling zone, not a functional endpoint. Use the queue line, the counter perimeter and the adjacent fixtures for gifts, candles, accessories, party items, paper products and seasonal add-ons — easy impulse purchases at the last decision point. Keep it premium, clear and easy to replenish; the queue is merchandising space, not dead space.

The presentation lookbook

Our page-by-page reference for how products are staged and photographed lives in a separate lookbook. Review it alongside this section — the showcase types above must be able to reproduce those compositions on the floor.

06

What we need from you.

D1

The layout

A plan of the whole unit on the measured drawing (Fig. 03) where every zone and the customer walk are clearly legible: the checkout with its Gifting / Party / Impulse zone, the packaging area, the office, the Villeroy & Boch corner, every category zone, the Home Consultation / Planning Area, Outdoor & Garden — and, most importantly, the main entrances and how they feed the circulation. The extension contingency drawn both on and off.

D2

The furniture & décor concept

A developed concept for the mood modules of Section 04: hero settings, high-capacity merchandising walls, décor and small-furniture showcases, the headboard / material gallery, your dining-table solution (Rule 05), and the integrated Home Consultation / Planning Area. Concept drawings, materials, and one module developed in full as the reference.

D3

The house fixture language

A coherent house fixture family informed by multiple benchmarks — CoinCasa, Zara Home, IKEA, Maisons du Monde — without reproducing any one retailer. Golden Apple is a behavioural reference only. The family must carry the boutique's own architectural language, material palette, detailing and finishes across both display languages.

D4

Checkout & cross-selling

A developed checkout concept: queue logic, the packaging interface, and a purposeful Gifting / Party / Impulse offer merchandised on the counter perimeter and queue line.

D5

Outdoor & Garden

A dedicated concept for outdoor furniture, garden tools, lawn-care equipment, lawnmowers and related categories — a technical assortment that must still read as the boutique — including how the zone converts seasonally to the Christmas shop on one flexible fixture skeleton.

D6

The technical package

Technical drawings suitable for local production of every fixture, plus the complete lighting design, and all POS architecture details: shelf talkers, price rails, ticket holders, mood identity bands, signage and wayfinding elements.

Questions, at any hour, to the Italdizain project team. Where this brief is silent, propose; where it is specific, challenge it if you disagree — but in writing, before drawing.
